title: Skills-first hiring: Credentials retain employer influence
desc: Frames workforce adaptation through training and inclusive talent practices while exposing tension between skills claims and conventional selection.

kps.k: The cluster frames AI workforce change as a skills and organisational adaptation challenge, not simply a displacement forecast.
kps.d: The Future of Jobs Report 2025 draws on employer survey evidence from 2024. Globally, 63% identify labour-market skills gaps and 46% identify organisational culture and resistance as barriers to business transformation generally. For AI adoption specifically, half of executives identify insufficient skills as the leading barrier, while 43% cite a lack of managerial and leadership vision. These findings describe perceived constraints and forward-looking expectations, not demonstrated causal effects of AI.

kps.k: Employers anticipate automation and augmentation together, and plan to combine training, hiring and redeployment.
kps.d: Global task shares move from 48% predominantly human, 30% combined human–technology and 22% predominantly technological at the survey baseline to an expected 33%, 33% and 34% in 2030. In response to AI, 77% of employers plan to reskill existing workers, 69% to hire AI-tool designers, 62% to hire people able to work alongside AI, and 47% to redeploy workers from declining roles internally. Another 49% plan to pursue AI-created business opportunities. This presents substitution and workforce development as concurrent strategies; task shares do not measure job losses, technology extends beyond AI, and planned transitions do not establish successful implementation.

kps.k: The principal tension concerns skills-first recruitment versus employers’ continued preference for experience and conventional credentials.
kps.d: The report argues that skills-first hiring and routes such as vocational training and apprenticeships can broaden talent pipelines. Yet 81% of respondents prioritise work experience, 48% pre-employment tests and 43% university degrees, compared with 17% for apprenticeships and 14% for short courses or online certificates. Expected use of these alternative credentials has declined slightly since the 2023 edition. This is a tension between the report’s recommendation and employer intentions, rather than a disagreement between independent sources; expanding training routes alone may not change how employers recognise skills.

kps.k: The practical agenda extends beyond technical training to retention, working conditions, inclusion and public support.
kps.d: Employers identify wellbeing, career progression, reskilling, higher wages, remote or hybrid work and broader recruitment pools as potential ways to improve talent availability. Globally, 55% identify public training funding and 52% training provision as promising policies. Separately, planned DEI measures include comprehensive training at 51%, targeted recruitment, retention and progression at 48%, and pay-equity reviews at 39%. These priorities suggest a multi-part workforce strategy, but the survey does not demonstrate that the measures improve inclusion, retention or AI adoption.

kps.k: The report supplies context for the legal-workforce debate, but does not support a lawyer-specific displacement estimate from these extracts.
kps.d: The labelled professional-services profile reports 95% of organisations running AI programmes, 41% core-skill disruption and 19% five-year labour-market churn, against global figures of 88%, 39% and 22%. Programme prevalence, expected skill change and churn measure different things; none directly measures lawyer job losses. Missing headings prevent secure interpretation of a separate lawyers row, and page transitions make adjacent sector labels unreliable guides to preceding tables. Legal-sector planning can use the broad adaptation themes, but cannot treat these figures as a forecast of law-firm staffing or realised AI productivity.

vlens.an: The supplied market-analysis source supports the proposition by framing AI-related workforce change primarily as a skills and organisational-adaptation challenge. It anticipates employers combining reskilling, AI-capable recruitment, redeployment, automation and augmentation rather than treating technological change solely as a displacement forecast. Most directly, it endorses skills-first hiring as a means of broadening talent pipelines while documenting the proposition’s central tension: surveyed employers remain much more likely to prioritise work experience, pre-employment tests and university degrees than apprenticeships or short-form credentials. This internal variation is a tension between the report’s recommendation and the employer intentions it records, not substantive opposition to the proposition. The source also limits the strength of its claims: the evidence concerns expectations and planned responses rather than realised outcomes, and its professional-services indicators do not establish lawyer-specific displacement. Because this facet contains one curated source, the finding characterises that source’s position and should not be treated as representative of market analysts, consultancies or the press generally.

elens.an: The 2025 source supports the proposition that workforce adaptation is being framed in skills-first terms while conventional credentials and selection mechanisms retain substantial employer influence. The report recommends broader pathways—including vocational training, apprenticeships, on-the-job experience and associate degrees—and presents reskilling, AI-capable recruitment and redeployment as responses to anticipated technological change. At the same time, its employer-survey evidence shows a marked gap between that recommendation and intended hiring practice: work experience, pre-employment tests and university degrees rank well above apprenticeships and short courses or online certificates. The report therefore treats AI-related workforce change primarily as a skills and organisational adaptation challenge, but indicates that expanding training routes alone may not alter how employers recognise skills. Material internal variation lies between the report’s normative endorsement of skills-first hiring and respondents’ stated assessment priorities; there is also variation across sector, regional and economy profiles in perceived skills and organisational barriers. These findings remain expectations and plans reported in a 2024 survey, not evidence of successful adoption, realised hiring changes or AI-caused displacement, and the professional-services extracts do not establish a lawyer-specific forecast.
